design_detail: Consensus committee report (13 members; chair David L. Eaton) commissioned by the US Food and Drug Administration through a contract with the National Academies, to review the health effects of e-cigarettes, smoking initiation and cessation, and harm reduction. Chapter 2 says the committee's approach 'incorporated major attributes of systematic reviews': a six-database search (collection from 1 February to 31 August 2017, no limits on date, language or country), predefined inclusion criteria (peer-reviewed original research on humans, animals or cells), study assessment by one committee member followed by whole-committee discussion, and a narrative synthesis. Findings are worded on a six-level scale (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, insufficient, no available evidence) and listed as 47 numbered conclusions. No pooled estimate is reported; the committee calculated one risk ratio itself (Chapter 10). A population model (Chapter 19) projects possible net effects. The report says it did not systematically review the health effects of individual constituents (nicotine, humectants, certain metals), which it takes from other literature. AMSTAR 2 is used because the report states a systematic search and selection (Chapter 2, Literature Search; Appendix B, Literature Search; Box B-2) for the studies behind the conclusions used here (Chapters 4, 9, 10, 11 and 18).
can_establish: What an expert committee concluded, at what stated level of evidence, about each of 47 questions on e-cigarettes as of a literature collection that ended on 31 August 2017; which kinds of studies (designs, sizes, follow-up) sat under each conclusion; and which outcomes had no human studies at all.
cannot_establish: The size of any risk or of any difference between e-cigarettes and smoking (the level of evidence 'does not indicate the size, magnitude, or importance of the effect', Chapter 2); anything published after August 2017 (including the PATH Study cohort papers on heart and lung disease in this batch); which studies were excluded and why (no list or count is printed); the health effects of nicotine itself (not systematically reviewed); long-term effects, since the longest human health follow-ups described are one to two years.

sample.recruitment: Searches in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO (ProQuest), MEDLINE (Ovid) and Embase (Ovid) between 1 February and 31 August 2017 with the terms e-cigarette(s), electronic cigarette(s), electronic nicotine delivery, electronic nicotine device, vape, vaping and e-liquid (MeSH term added in PubMed and MEDLINE), plus special searches on dependence, smoking initiation, cessation (reviews and original studies) and smoking reduction. Appendix B gives the first series of six searches (1 to 6 February 2017) and the dependence search (14 July to 31 August) as five databases, the smoking-transition searches (to March or May 2017) as six or seven, and 641 further unique results from updates to 31 August. For smoking transitions the committee first assessed existing systematic reviews and then added newer studies. A professional research librarian helped; titles and abstracts were screened with criteria developed in a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Chapter 2, Literature Search; Appendix B, Literature Search).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Box B-2: human, animal or cell studies; exposure to e-cigarettes or their products; any physiological response or biological effect as outcome; peer-reviewed original research. For the harm-reduction chapter: studies of people who switched from smoking were included only if e-cigarette use was the treatment condition and smoking the positive control; studies that calculated risk from known toxicant risks in other settings were excluded; cross-sectional studies and case reports were excluded from the health-outcome analysis (15 longitudinal or crossover studies); studies that compared people who use e-cigarettes with historical data from other studies were excluded for dual use and secondhand exposure (Chapter 18, Evidence Review: Methods).
sample.demographics: Not summarised across the report. Chapter 9 gives mean ages of 23 to 39 years in the short-term clinical studies (healthy adults, mostly without hypertension or diabetes risk factors) and 33 to 54 years in the longer-term studies, with recruitment sites in Italy, Greece, Poland, Sweden and several US cities.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at report level; in the studies described, losses to follow-up were large in some (for example 17 of 40 in a 24-month study of people not intending to quit; the Catania cohort in Chapter 9 has 'a relatively large loss of study participants during follow-up').
sample.selection_effects: Literature collection ended on 31 August 2017 (the smoking-transition searches ran to March or May 2017, plus updates), so the report predates the large national cohorts (such as the PATH Study papers in this batch). Chapter 4 mentions nicotine-salt devices only briefly: a chemical analysis of one pod product, and a clinical pharmacokinetic study of a prototype developed by Philip Morris Products S.A. Most human studies were small, short and in healthy adults, mostly with first- or second-generation devices. Six of the 17 respiratory studies came from one research group, and most of the benefit studies from one region of Italy (Chapter 11). The committee prioritised human studies for its most structured assessments and used animal and cell studies as supporting evidence. Peer-reviewed papers only; no grey-literature or registry search is described.

exposure.measurement: E-cigarette devices and e-liquids as used in each study, from first-generation 'cigalikes' to tank and variable-power devices; exposure assessed by biomarkers of exposure (urinary nicotine equivalents, cotinine, the tobacco-specific nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, volatile organic compound metabolites, exhaled carbon monoxide), laboratory emissions, and in some cohorts by self-report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inhaled aerosol. In the study conditions read: e-liquid nicotine from none to 36 mg/ml in controlled sessions of 10 to 15 puffs or ad libitum use of 60 to 90 minutes; switching studies lasted from 5 days to 12 weeks (one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months), and observational cohorts up to 24 months. The Chapter 4 synthesis says nicotine yield increases with device power, e-liquid nicotine concentration and puff duration.
exposure.polysubstance: Chapters separate people who have never smoked, people who currently or formerly smoked, dual use and exclusive e-cigarette use; the report says dual use may confer benefit only if it is transitional and that the health effects of dual use over the long term are not known (Chapter 18). Cannabis vaping is not part of the report's scope.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Laboratory sessions often required hours of abstinence from smoking or e-cigarette use (Chapter 9). In free-living switching studies compliance was checked by exhaled carbon monoxide or self-report and was incomplete (in the 12-week Cravo trial 40.2% were compliant, defined as self-reported smoking no cigarettes on 80% or more of study days) (Chapter 4; Chapter 18).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: smoking as positive control, no use, nicotine-free e-cigarettes, sham puffing, nicotine replacement, and continued smoking. The committee's own list of preferred comparison groups for future studies is people who continue to smoke, people trying to quit with other evidence-based treatments, and people who use no tobacco products including e-cigarettes (Box S-4, Recommendation 15-2).
comparison.matching: Crossover designs in most short-term clinical studies; matching in a few cohorts (for example, a hypertension cohort matched for age, sex and blood-pressure stability). Not applicable at report level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Chapter 9 notes that the Moheimani 2017 comparison did not adjust for sociodemographic characteristics or cardiovascular risk factors; Chapter 10 notes no consideration of complete smoking history or confounders in the Manzoli data, and that the e-cigarette group in Franco 2016 was on average 10 years older than the other groups.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking history is the main concern raised in the chapters read. The respiratory chapter names dual tobacco or cannabinoid use, secondhand smoke exposure and prior tobacco use as confounders to consider (Chapter 11, Optimal Study Design, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Biomarkers of exposure and potential harm; heart rate, blood pressure, arterial stiffness, flow-mediated dilation; spirometry and symptom questionnaires; self-reported adverse events; in animals and cells, cytotoxicity, inflammation and DNA damage.
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was judged qualitatively (design, sample, comparison groups, statistics, outcome measures, confounding, loss to follow-up, sponsorship); no named risk-of-bias tool, per-study rating or reliability data are printed for the health-effect studies. For the Franco 2016 micronucleus study the chapter notes that evidence on the assay's reliability was not presented.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No available evidence' means no studies at all; 'insufficient' means mixed findings or a single poor study; 'limited', 'moderate', 'substantial' and 'conclusive' describe a direction of effect with increasing support (Box S-2; Chapter 2, Conclusions).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. The committee calculated one risk ratio itself, for 'any cancer' reported among serious adverse events over 24 months in the Manzoli cohort: 2/97 for e-cigarette only against 3/363 for smoking only, risk ratio 2.49 (95% CI 0.42 to 14.72), which the chapter calls 'extremely limited by sample size' and of low quality (Chapter 10). Ranges quoted from single studies include a fall in the urinary nitrosamine metabolite NNAL of 57% after one week and 64% after two weeks in 20 people who switched (Chapter 18). The conclusion levels themselves do not carry effect sizes.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is described. The Statement of Task (summarised in Summary Box S-1; Chapter 1 not read) set the scope; inclusion criteria were developed through a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Appendix B); no deviations are discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be checked: no list or count of excluded studies, and the number of studies behind most conclusions is not stated. The sponsorship table for included studies is in an online supplement that was not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Human studies quoted for exposure and short-term health outcomes range from 13 to 420 people; the Manzoli cohort is given as 932 or 1,355, and a cross-sectional survey of college students (Loukas) as 5,468 (Chapters 9, 10, 11, 18).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As of studies to August 2017: no human studies of clinical heart disease, stroke or atherosclerosis (Conclusion 9-1), of cancer (10-1) or of respiratory disease (11-1) in people who use e-cigarettes; short-term rises in heart rate (substantial) and diastolic blood pressure (moderate) after nicotine intake; lower exposure to many toxicants and carcinogens in people who completely switched from smoking (conclusive) in studies of 13 to 420 people lasting 2 to 12 weeks; limited evidence of better lung function in adults with asthma and fewer exacerbations in adults with COPD after switching, mostly from one research group; moderate evidence of more cough and wheeze in adolescents in four cross-sectional studies; no available evidence (long-term) and insufficient evidence (short-term) on health outcomes in people who use both products.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says laboratory tests, in vitro tests and short-term human studies 'suggest that e-cigarettes are likely to be far less harmful than combustible tobacco cigarettes', while 'the absolute risks of the products cannot be unambiguously determined' and long-term effects are not yet clear; it also says e-cigarette constituents are 'not inert' and likely to have some negative health effects on their own. The Chapter 18 synthesis says all but one human study showed significant short-term improvements in people who smoked and switched, and calls the improvement consistent across all studies, which is stronger than the studies it describes (see reporting issues). Statements about nicotine itself (minimal cancer risk; likely higher cardiovascular risk in people with existing heart disease) are not graded conclusions.

timeline.event: McKee and Capewell, 'Evidence about electronic cigarettes: A foundation built on rock or sand?' (BMJ), is cited by the committee in Chapter 18 for concerns about using e-cigarettes for harm reduction (continued use of a product with its own risks, possible increases in smoking, and terms of engagement with the tobacco industry). It was not read for this card.

McNeill and colleagues, Nicotine vaping in England: 2022 evidence update, commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; an independent review with a later search date (card sc_mcneill_2022).

Banks and colleagues' umbrella and systematic review takes this report as its starting point; 112 of its 400 publications come from it, so the two are not independent (card sc_banks_2023). It rates clinical heart disease and cancer 'no available evidence' and rates the certainty of cardiovascular and respiratory findings low or very low.

replication.where_it_stands: Not independently replicated as a review. A later umbrella review (Banks 2023) uses this report's studies as a base, so it is not independent of it. On clinical heart disease and cancer its 'no available evidence' ratings describe the 2017 literature; later cohort studies exist (see sc_berlowitz_2022 and sc_xie_2020) but were outside its search. A critique of the later review (Mendelsohn 2022) is listed in the library and was not read.

funding.funder: US Food and Drug Administration. The front matter on the book's landing page prints the sponsor statement: support under contract number HHSF223201610054C between the National Academy of Sciences and the US Department of Health and Human Services (Food and Drug Administration), and adds that opinions in the report do not necessarily reflect the views of any organization or agency that provided support. The FDA's Center for Tobacco Products asked the National Academies to convene the committee (Summary, opening, 7th paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: No statement of committee members' financial interests, or of how they were managed, appears in the pages read (landing page, committee list, Reviewers, Preface, Summary, Chapter 2, Appendix B, Appendix F biosketches). Appendix B says that where committee members co-authored studies under review, members who did not take part in the study reviewed them independently; committee members Goniewicz and St.Helen are authors of studies reviewed in Chapters 4, 5, 9, 10 and 18. Chapter 2 (footnote 3) and Appendix B say the committee recorded each study's sponsor (industry, government or federal agency, other, not stated) and any other industry involvement in an online table, which was not read. The Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre, as printed, and a reviewer (Hecht) who is an author of a study reviewed in Chapter 18. In the chapter text, some studies are named by commercial product (blu, SKYCIG, Vype ePen, Green Smoke) and one trial's product is described as developed by Fontem Ventures B.V.; the sponsors are in the unread table.
funding.affiliations_note: Committee members are from US universities and medical centres (Washington, South Carolina, Roswell Park, USC, Connecticut, Johns Hopkins, Michigan, Columbia, UC Davis, Harvard/MGH, Brown, UCSF), as printed in the committee list. The commissioning agency regulates e-cigarettes as tobacco products (Summary, opening, 7th paragraph).

what_would_settle_it: An update of the same review with a search beyond 2017 that includes the large longitudinal cohorts and any trials with clinical endpoints, with a registered protocol, duplicate screening, a published list of excluded studies, study-level risk-of-bias ratings, and comparison groups named in advance (people who continue to smoke, people using other cessation treatments, and people using no tobacco products). The committee itself lists such studies as research needs (Boxes S-3 to S-5).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The Statement of Task names populations (people who use the products, vulnerable groups, people exposed to secondhand aerosol), the exposure and the outcomes; Box B-2 lists exposure and outcome but no comparator. Comparison groups are chosen chapter by chapter.
No protocol is described; inclusion criteria were developed during a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Appendix B).

Chapter 2 and Appendix B explain the design hierarchy (randomized trials, controlled studies, prospective cohorts and crossover trials, case reports for injuries), why human studies were prioritised, and why animal and cell studies were used as supporting evidence.

Six databases, search terms and syntax printed (Boxes B-1A to B-7), no language or date limits; no reference-list, registry, grey-literature or expert search is described, and the databases differ between Chapter 2 (six for the whole period) and Appendix B (five for the first series).
Titles and abstracts were reviewed against criteria; the number of reviewers is not stated.

One committee member made the initial review of the studies for a set of outcomes, and the full committee then discussed each assessment (Chapter 2). That is a consensus check, not independent duplicate extraction as AMSTAR 2 defines it; a more lenient reader could judge it differently.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list, no count of full texts assessed or excluded, and no reasons are printed in Chapter 2 or Appendix B; only counts of unique search results are given.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Chapter text and Tables 4-2, 9-1, 9-2 and 11-1 give device, e-liquid, sample, setting, protocol, follow-up and outcomes (tables are images and were not extracted; the chapter text was read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Qualitative appraisal that names confounding, sampling, loss to follow-up, outcome operationalization and sponsorship (Appendix B, Quality Assessment); no tool is named and no per-study judgments are shown.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Chapter 2 (footnote 3) and Appendix B say sponsorship of every included study was recorded in an online supplement table, which was not read.
No meta-analysis; existing meta-analyses were assessed for the smoking-transition questions.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The level-of-evidence scale is tied to study quality and the chapters name limits of each body of evidence (for example Chapter 9: no adjustment for sociodemographic factors in some studies; Chapter 11: one research group, retrospective selection).
Differences between studies are discussed (for example heart-rate findings by device generation and nicotine delivery; inconsistent systolic blood pressure findings).
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed in the chapters read.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The FDA contract is printed; no statement of the committee members' own interests or of how they were managed was found in the pages read; Appendix B describes how studies co-authored by members were reviewed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 10 can be judged only from the online sponsorship table, which was not read; it is non-critical and cannot change the overall rating. The rating rests on two critical items judged 'no' from the pages read: no protocol (item 2) and no list or count of excluded studies (item 7). AMSTAR 2 was built for reviews of intervention trials and gives 'critically low' to any review with more than one critical flaw; here the flaws are reproducibility and reporting ones in a transparent consensus report, and the rating does not say the graded conclusions are wrong. The report may be cited for the committee's judgment and its stated level of evidence, for the kinds and sizes of studies under each conclusion, and for the places where it says no human studies existed (clinical heart disease, cancer, respiratory disease, long-term dual use); not for effect sizes, for completeness of the literature, for anything after August 2017, or as independent confirmation of the later reviews that start from it.

verification.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML of NBK507171 (nap24952), read 2026-10-18 in a browser tab: landing page (sponsor statement and suggested citation), committee list, Reviewers, Preface, Summary in full with Boxes S-1 to S-5, Summary Annex (all 47 conclusions), Chapter 2 in full, Appendix B in full with Box B-2, Appendix F (biosketches), Chapter 4 (nicotine exposure sections in detail, nicotine salts, synthesis), Chapter 5 (introduction, carbonyl compounds, minor alkaloids, tobacco-specific nitrosamines, other toxicants, synthesis, metals; not humectants or flavorings in full), Chapter 9 in full, Chapter 10 (opening, optimal study design, epidemiology, case reports and synthesis; the animal and in vitro sections only skimmed), Chapter 11 (human studies, synthesis and conclusions, vulnerable populations; the animal and in vitro sections only skimmed), Chapter 18 in full. Not read: Chapters 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12 to 17 and 19 to 21, Appendixes A, C, D and E, Boxes B-1A to B-1F and B-3 to B-7 (search syntax), the tables and figures (shown as images), the online sponsorship supplement and the PDF. Reader 72 reads Chapters 3 and 8.

key_findings.finding: Mandate and method: Chapter 2 says the Statement of Task charges the committee with a 'comprehensive and systematic assessment and review of the literature' (the Summary's Box S-1 words the task as a comprehensive review of the literature on constituents, human health effects, initiation and cessation, and harm reduction). The committee searched six databases between 1 February and 31 August 2017 with no date, language or country limits (3,494 unique results in the first series, plus special searches on dependence, smoking initiation, cessation and smoking reduction, and 641 more through updates), assessed studies against criteria developed in a preliminary screen, and states it 'identified more than 800 peer-reviewed scientific studies' for the report. The Preface says that, where feasible, the committee applied the most important attributes of systematic review methodology.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Box S-1; Chapter 2, 1st paragraph and Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Literature Search, all subsections; Box B-2; Preface, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Appraisal: one committee member made an initial review of all studies for a set of outcomes, then the whole committee discussed each assessment, weighing design, sample, setting, comparison groups, statistics, outcome measures, confounding, loss to follow-up, other sources of bias and sponsorship; studies co-authored by committee members were reviewed by members who did not take part; case reports and animal or cell studies were assessed by modified approaches; existing reviews of smoking transitions were assessed with methods adapted from published guidelines. No named tool, per-study rating or list of excluded studies is printed; the sponsorship of each included study is recorded in an online table.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 2 › Literature Review and Quality Assessment › Health Effects Literature, 1st to 3rd paragraphs and footnote 3; Smoking Transitions Literature, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Quality Assessment (all subsections) and External Influences

key_findings.finding: Scale of evidence: conclusive (many supportive findings from good-quality controlled studies, no credible opposing findings), substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality observational studies or controlled trials), moderate (several findings from fair-quality studies), limited (supportive findings from fair-quality studies, or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion), insufficient (mixed findings or a single poor study; no conclusion can be made) and no available evidence (no studies). The committee states that the level 'does not indicate the size, magnitude, or importance of the effect' and that conclusions of insufficient or no available evidence 'do not imply a direction'. Across the 47 conclusions the Annex lists 8 conclusive, 10 substantial, 8 moderate, 12 limited, 4 insufficient and 5 no available evidence (reader's count of the Annex).
key_findings.locator: Summary › Box S-2; Chapter 2 › Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Headline: laboratory tests of ingredients, in vitro tests and short-term human studies 'suggest that e-cigarettes are likely to be far less harmful than combustible tobacco cigarettes', but 'the absolute risks of the products cannot be unambiguously determined' and the long-term effects, of particular concern for young people who become dependent, are not yet clear. The Summary also says e-cigarettes contain constituents that are 'not inert' and likely to have some negative health effects on their own, and that, because the risks of smoking are so great, the net effect depends on the relationship between e-cigarette use and smoking as well as on the products' own risks. The net public health effect depends on three factors: effect on initiation of smoking by young people, effect on cessation by adults, and intrinsic toxicity. Final observations: compared with cigarettes, e-cigarettes contain fewer toxicants, can deliver nicotine in a similar manner, show significantly less biological activity in a number of in vitro, animal and human systems and might be useful as a cessation aid to people who use them exclusively; but young people who begin with e-cigarettes are more likely to move to smoking, e-cigarettes can explode, and e-liquids are dangerous and can be fatal. 'Much of the research on e-cigarettes suffers from methodological flaws', and many areas are unstudied.
key_findings.locator: Summary, opening paragraphs 1, 2 and 5; Summary › Final Observations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Context from national surveys (Summary): youth e-cigarette use in 2016 was substantially higher than cigarette smoking; adult use was relatively low compared with youth use and adult smoking; most adults who use e-cigarettes report currently using other tobacco products; few adults begin using e-cigarettes without already smoking. In the cardiovascular studies of Chapter 9, all participants were current smokers in seven studies and some were in five more.
key_findings.locator: Summary, opening paragraph 4; Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine exposure: highly variable and dependent on product and how the device is operated (Conclusion 4-1, conclusive); nicotine intake among adults experienced with e-cigarettes can be comparable to that from cigarettes (4-2, substantial). Behind them: 27 acute clinical studies of nicotine exposure (17 in people who smoke with no or little experience of e-cigarettes and 12 in people with experience; these add to 29, so two studies appear in both groups, a reader's inference), in which blood nicotine in people new to e-cigarettes was much lower than from their usual cigarettes and in experienced people could reach the range of a typical cigarette; and seven switching studies, of which three reported no significant change in nicotine exposure and four suggested that some e-cigarettes were ineffective nicotine delivery devices compared with cigarettes. The Chapter 4 synthesis adds that nicotine yield rises with device power, e-liquid nicotine and puff duration. The Summary states that nicotine causes dependence and addiction.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph and Conclusions 4-1 and 4-2; Chapter 4 › Exposure to Nicotine and Nicotine Derivatives from E-Cigarettes, 3rd paragraph; Clinical Studies with E-Cigarette-Naive Smokers, 1st and last paragraphs; Clinical Studies in people experienced with e-cigarettes (the section after the one on people new to them), 1st and last paragraphs; Switching Studies, last paragraph; Synthesis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other toxicants: most products contain and emit numerous potentially toxic substances besides nicotine (5-1, conclusive); the number and amount vary widely with product and operation (5-2, conclusive); except for nicotine, under typical conditions of use, exposure to potentially toxic substances is significantly lower than from combustible tobacco cigarettes (5-3, substantial). Chapter 18 presents four direct comparisons: one calculation from published data found levels of selected toxicants in smoke 9 to 450 times those in aerosol, assuming 15 puffs per cigarette; one measured 150 chemicals and found toxicants 82 to more than 99% lower per puff in the e-cigarette aerosol; one found about 1,500 times more harmful or potentially harmful constituents in smoke; one compared 11 metals (higher in the aerosol for four, within the smoke range for five, lower for two). The Summary says that, taken together, the aerosol contains fewer numbers and lower levels of toxicants than smoke, and that exposure from flavorings and humectants depends on the characteristics of the person using the product and of the device.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, Conclusions 5-1 to 5-3 and closing paragraph; Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Nitrosamines and carbonyls: tobacco-specific nitrosamines were found in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, 'typically at levels similar to' those in pharmaceutical nicotine products (the chapter says this is probably attributed to pharmaceutical-grade nicotine); one study of 12 brands found two nitrosamines in aerosol from all but three, and another, of three liquids, found none in 100-puff aerosol. Carbonyls such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein were found in aerosol and were in most cases lower than in smoke (for example 86 to 544 times lower for three carbonyls in one comparison), but very high formaldehyde levels were also reported, one study estimated formaldehyde exposure comparable to a cigarette, and levels varied widely between brands and between samples of the same product.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Tobacco-Specific Nitrosamines, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Carbonyl Compounds, 2nd to 11th paragraphs; Chapter 10, opening, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Metals: aerosol contains metals from the coil, other parts of the device and the liquid (5-4, substantial); the number of metals could be greater than in cigarette smoke, except for cadmium, which is markedly lower (5-5, limited). The chapter notes few, mostly small studies of first- and second-generation devices, metal levels that 'can be substantially high in some instances', one biomarker study of 64 people supporting an inhaled contribution to the internal dose of chromium and nickel, and no study of the health effects of metals from e-cigarettes except one cell study of copper nanoparticles.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, Conclusions 5-4 and 5-5; Chapter 5 › Metals, 6th and 8th paragraphs and Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Exposure falls when people switch completely (18-1, conclusive). The Synthesis says all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who substituted e-cigarettes for cigarettes, and that nicotine intake among people experienced with e-cigarettes was comparable to that from cigarettes. Examples: a 5-day randomized study of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29 to 95% lower and exhaled carbon monoxide 27 to 89% lower after partial or complete switching; people who used both products and replaced half their cigarettes had 7 to 38% reductions and 1 to 20% higher nicotine equivalents); 20 people switched for two weeks (NNAL 57% lower after one week and 64% after two; total nicotine and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites unchanged at one week); 40 people followed for four weeks, 33 of whom were using e-cigarettes at the end (48% only e-cigarettes, 52% both products; exhaled carbon monoxide 80% lower with e-cigarettes only and 52% lower with both products; the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 79% and 60% lower); a cross-sectional comparison of 181 people in five groups (36 or 37 each) in which long-term exclusive e-cigarette use had lower NNAL than every other group, while nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who used both products were similar to those in people who only smoked. Studies ranged from 13 to 420 people with follow-up of 2 to 12 weeks, apart from one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months. The 12-week trial of a manufacturer's product (developed by Fontem Ventures B.V., per Chapter 18) had 40.2% compliance in its unconfined phase.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Harm Reduction, Conclusion 18-1; Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 10th paragraphs and Synthesis; Chapter 4 › Switching Studies, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Short-term health outcomes after complete switching (18-2, substantial). The Synthesis says all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in respiratory, cardiovascular and oral outcomes, in most studies in relatively small numbers of people; 21 of 27 in vitro studies and 3 of 5 animal studies favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful and none found them more harmful. One 2-week pilot of 20 people found a statistically significant increase in gum inflammation after switching. For people who keep smoking while using e-cigarettes: no available evidence on long-term illness or death compared with smoking only (18-3) and insufficient evidence on short-term outcomes (18-4); the chapter adds that on average they do not smoke fewer cigarettes (though among them e-cigarettes 'may help maintain smoking reduction') and that those who do not reduce smoking are very unlikely to reduce risk and may be exposed to additional effects of e-cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Harm Reduction, Conclusions 18-2 to 18-4; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, last paragraph (Wadia 2016); Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently, Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Harm-reduction framing: the committee says e-cigarettes 'have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe' but may be less harmful alternatives to smoking in at least some scenarios; those who switch completely would be expected to gain more than those who keep smoking, and dual use may confer benefit only if it is a transitional state; the evidence about harm reduction suggests that across a range of studies and outcomes e-cigarettes 'pose less risk to an individual than combustible tobacco cigarettes'. Modeling (Summary): a net public health benefit in the short run if adult cessation increases, substantially less and negative under some scenarios at 50 years, and net harm in the short and long terms if the products do not increase adult cessation.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 18, opening, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Summary › Harm Reduction, last paragraph; Summary › Modeling, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heart and circulation: no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis (9-1); heart rate rises shortly after nicotine intake (9-2, substantial); diastolic blood pressure rises (9-3, moderate); limited evidence for short-term rises in systolic blood pressure, oxidative stress markers, endothelial dysfunction, arterial stiffness and autonomic changes (9-4); insufficient evidence for long-term changes in heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac geometry and function (9-5). Behind them: 13 short-term clinical studies (2010 to 2017; mostly crossover; healthy adults aged 23 to 39 on average) and three longer studies (a 34-person cross-sectional study; a randomized cessation trial analysed as a cohort, 183 people; a record-based cohort of 89 hypertensive patients); none measured clinical or subclinical atherosclerosis outcomes. The chapter says the five studies finding no heart-rate change (2010 to 2014) used first- or second-generation devices with small or no rises in nicotine biomarkers, and the five finding a rise (2015 to 2017) used tank-style or participants' own devices or showed a nicotine rise; effects were generally smaller than with cigarettes but closer for some products with higher nicotine intake; diastolic pressure rises were similar in size to those after a cigarette.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 9-1 to 9-5; Chapter 9 › Characterization of Disease Endpoints and Intermediate Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Heart Rate, 1st paragraph and Synthesis; Blood Pressure, Synthesis; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Cancer: no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with intermediate cancer endpoints in humans, compared with smoking or with no tobacco use (10-1); the chapter says the literature is 'devoid' of rigorous epidemiology on intermediate cancer endpoints, let alone cancer. The two human studies that refer to cancer were a 24-month cohort in which 'any cancer' was reported under serious adverse events (presumably self-reported; 2/97 e-cigarette only, 3/363 smoking only, 0/37 using both; committee-calculated risk ratio 2.49, 95% CI 0.42 to 14.72, called extremely limited by sample size and low quality) and a 65-person micronucleus study of cells scraped from the mouth (micronucleated cells 21% higher, and total micronuclei 133% higher, in people who used e-cigarettes than in people who neither smoked nor used them, against 160% and 633% higher in people who smoked; the e-cigarette group was on average 10 years older and the chapter notes no evidence on the assay's reliability). Limited evidence from animal studies using intermediate biomarkers that long-term use could increase cancer risk, and none from long-term animal bioassays (10-2); limited evidence of mutagenicity or DNA damage (10-3); substantial evidence that formaldehyde and acrolein can cause DNA damage (10-4), which supports biological plausibility but not a risk estimate. The statements about nicotine itself are not graded conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 10-1 to 10-4; Chapter 10 › Optimal Study Design, 1st paragraph; Epidemiology, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Synthesis; Chapter 4 › Synthesis, 2nd paragraph; Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lungs: no available evidence whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease in humans (11-1); limited evidence for better lung function and symptoms in adults who smoke and have asthma after switching completely or partly (11-2) and for fewer COPD exacerbations (11-3), from small studies selected retrospectively, mostly one region of Italy, with the one randomized trial (12 weeks) finding no lung-function difference; moderate evidence for more cough and wheeze in adolescents and an association with asthma exacerbations (11-4), from four cross-sectional self-reported studies; limited animal and cell evidence of harm (11-5). The chapter says studies of long-term effects on chronic respiratory symptoms are 'completely lacking', that results are unclear whether use instead of smoking in people with COPD may be beneficial, neutral or harmful, and, in its synthesis, that nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can have short-term adverse effects on lung defences (mucociliary clearance, urge to cough, cough sensitivity; moderate evidence, not carried to a numbered conclusion). The Summary adds that use instead of smoking by people with existing respiratory disease 'might be less harmful'.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 11-1 to 11-5 and closing paragraph; Chapter 11 › Clinical and Epidemiological Studies in Humans › the section on people who use combustible tobacco products, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Respiratory Symptoms in Adolescents; Synthesis and Conclusions, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Vulnerable/Susceptible Populations › COPD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other conclusions listed in the Summary: acute endothelial cell dysfunction (7-1) and oxidative stress (7-2) substantial; symptoms of dependence on e-cigarettes substantial (8-1), dependence risk and severity lower than for cigarettes moderate (8-2), product characteristics an important determinant moderate (8-3); periodontal improvement after switching limited and oral cell damage limited (12-1, 12-2); pregnancy outcomes no available evidence and fetal development insufficient (13-1, 13-2); explosions, burns, poisoning from e-liquids and fatal exposure conclusive (14-1 to 14-3); indoor air nicotine and particulate matter conclusive (3-1) and nicotine and other constituents on indoor surfaces limited (3-2); secondhand nicotine and particulate exposure lower than from smoking, moderate (18-5). The Summary's closing statement on health effects: e-cigarettes are 'not without physiological activity in humans', and the long-term implications for illness and death are not yet clear. Chapters 3, 7, 8 and 12 to 14 were not read.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents and Human Health Effects and Harm Reduction, Conclusions 3-1, 3-2, 7-1 to 8-3, 12-1 to 14-3, 18-5; Summary › Human Health Effects, closing paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Smoking initiation and cessation (listed for completeness; Chapters 16 and 17 not read): e-cigarette use increases the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people (16-1, substantial), the frequency and intensity of later smoking (16-2, moderate) and, in the near term, its duration (16-3, limited); limited overall evidence that e-cigarettes may be effective cessation aids (17-1); moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes beat nicotine-free ones in randomized trials (17-2); insufficient evidence against no treatment or approved treatments (17-3); moderate evidence from observational studies that more frequent use goes with a higher likelihood of cessation, while the overall observational evidence is mixed (17-4). The Summary states that, taken together, e-cigarettes might cause young people to move on to smoking and might increase adult cessation.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Initiation and Cessation, Conclusions 16-1 to 17-4 and closing paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Research needs (Boxes S-3 to S-5): study the stability and heated by-products of e-liquid ingredients; indoor air quality and secondhand exposure in vulnerable groups; particle deposition in the airways; longitudinal cohorts of young people with little or no smoking; abuse-liability testing; and in clinical and epidemiological studies comparison groups of people who continue to smoke, people who try to quit with other evidence-based treatments, and people who use no tobacco products including e-cigarettes. The Summary says gaps were found in every aspect of the committee's work.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Research Recommendations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Boxes S-3, S-4 and S-5

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction synthesis says all but one human study showed significant short-term improvements in people who smoked and switched, and that the improvement was consistent across all studies, but studies described in the same section report no significant change (Cibella 2016: no differences in spirometry except one flow measure; D'Ruiz 2017: non-significant improvements in lung volumes; Szołtysek-Bołdys 2014: no significant changes in arterial stiffness, blood pressure or heart rate; Cravo 2016: no clinically significant product-related findings, which is absence of harm rather than improvement).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched › Health Risk Profile, 3rd, 4th, 8th and 14th paragraphs; Synthesis, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Conclusion 18-2 (substantial) should be cited with its level and with the sizes and durations of the studies behind it, not as a finding that every study improved.

reporting_issues.issue: The same study of arterial stiffness (Szołtysek-Bołdys 2014) is described differently in two chapters: Chapter 9 reports that the stiffness index fell after a cigarette (p = 0.006) but not after an e-cigarette; Chapter 18 says there were 'no significant changes' after the cigarette while printing p = 0.0056 and p = 0.010 for the same comparison, and gives 6.75 as the after value and 6.56 as the before value, the reverse of Chapter 9.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 9 › Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Endothelial Function, and Arterial Stiffness, 4th paragraph; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, 14th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the cigarette comparison in this study cannot be taken from Chapter 18.

reporting_issues.issue: Cibella 2016 (300 people, Catania group) is described as an observational study of people not intending to quit who were invited to switch in Chapter 11, and as a 1-year randomized controlled trial in which groups of 'quitters', 'reducers' and 'failures' are compared in Chapter 18; Chapter 9 describes the Farsalinos 2016 Catania cohort as a randomized trial also analysed as a cohort, with the same three labels and nicotine arms (the chapters do not say whether it is the same trial).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 11 › Clinical and Epidemiological Studies in Humans, 1st paragraph; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, 3rd paragraph; Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Groups formed by what people did after assignment are not randomized comparisons; the design behind the limited conclusions 11-2 and 11-3 is hard to pin down from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: The Manzoli cohort is described as 932 people with end-of-follow-up groups of 363, 97 and 37 (which add to 497) in Chapter 10, and as 1,355 people with 343 using e-cigarettes only and 319 using both products in Chapter 18.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Epidemiology, 1st paragraph; Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind the committee's own risk ratio for cancer cannot be reconciled from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 9 counts 13 short-term clinical studies and three longer studies (16) but then refers to 15 studies; its totals (356 + 306 = 662 participants) agree with the three longer studies (34 + 183 + 89 = 306). It also says five studies enrolled people experienced with e-cigarettes but cites two.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The study count behind the cardiovascular conclusions is uncertain by one; the participant total is consistent with 16 studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 2 and the opening of Appendix B give six databases (including Embase) for 1 February to 31 August 2017, but Appendix B's account of the first series of six searches (1 to 6 February 2017, 3,494 results) and of the dependence search lists five (no Embase), the cessation review search lists seven, and the databases for the 641 update results are not listed.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 2 › Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Health Effects of E-Cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; E-Cigarettes and Transitions to and from Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoking; Literature Updates
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether Embase was searched for the health-effects and exposure literature.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-3 (lower toxicant exposure) closes the Chapter 5 synthesis, which cites no comparison studies; the direct comparisons are partly in Chapter 5's carbonyl and metals sections and mainly in Chapter 18, which Chapter 5 itself points to. Chapter 5 also reports one study estimating formaldehyde exposure comparable to a cigarette.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 5 › Synthesis; Chapter 5 › Carbonyl Compounds, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels, Synthesis
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Chapter 18 for the four direct comparisons and Chapter 5 for the variability and the high-formaldehyde reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The synthesis of Chapter 11 states moderate evidence of short-term adverse effects of nicotine-containing e-cigarettes on lung defence mechanisms, but none of the five numbered respiratory conclusions (11-1 to 11-5) carries it.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 11 › Synthesis and Conclusions, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions 11-1 to 11-5
reporting_issues.consequence: The graded short-term lung-defence finding is not in the Annex's list of 47 conclusions and cannot be cited by number.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements on nicotine itself (minimal cancer risk from e-cigarette nicotine; likely higher cardiovascular risk in people with existing disease; uncertain risk in people without) are not graded conclusions and rest on other literature that the committee says it did not review systematically.
reporting_issues.locator: Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph; Chapter 2 › Smoking Transitions Literature, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 4 › Synthesis, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite these as the committee's reading, not as graded evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 4 text gives 419 enrolled in the 12-week Cravo trial; Chapter 18 gives 420 people who smoke.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 4 › Switching Studies, 4th paragraph; Chapter 18 › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 3rd paragraph
